 BTC USD Price Analysis: The Mining Cost and $62,300 Sit Together 
 CryptoQuant founder Ki Young Ju noted that Bitcoin (BTC USD) has fallen to the price it costs to mine one Bitcoin. His chart, built from MARA Holdings’ filings, puts the miner’s average cost at $62,862 per coin in the third quarter. Bitcoin dipped to $62,063 on Wednesday and trades near $63,900 on Thursday.
 “A break below could pressure public miners and their institutional backers,” Ki wrote on X . Below that price, a miner spends more to produce a coin than the coin is worth.
 We checked how that line held up before. Bitcoin closed below $62,862 on 18 days since January 2025, all between June and August of this year. Each time, it was back above the line within a month.
 This time, though, two forces push the other way: MARA is selling its Bitcoin, and ETF investors are pulling money out.
 BTC USD Below Mining Cost: What Happened the Last Six Times
 We compared Binance’s daily BTC USD closes since January 2025 with the $62,862 line. Bitcoin dropped below it in six separate stretches, all this summer.
 Short dips: five of the six stretches lasted one or two days, in early June, July and on August 1.
 The long one: from June 23 to July 3, Bitcoin closed below cost 11 days in a row. It hit $57,800 on July 1, its lowest price of the past year.
 The recovery: 30 days after each stretch ended, Bitcoin was back above the line, but only by 1% to 3% in five cases. The exception was August 1, which was followed by a 25% rally to over $78,000.
 So the mining cost has acted as a floor, but a soft one. It stopped the falls without starting a rally, until August.
 The cost line also moves. MARA’s cost was close to $60,000 in the second quarter, so this summer’s dips were tested against a slightly lower bar than today’s.

 MARA Is Selling, and ETF Investors Are Leaving
 Two groups that usually support the price are selling instead.
 MARA: the largest listed miner sold 13,597 BTC for about $1.1 billion over six weeks, at an average of about $81,000, roughly 29% above its own mining cost. It said it would keep selling to fund AI data centers. At today’s price, that margin has shrunk to about 2%.
 Spot Bitcoin ETFs: these funds, which hold the coin itself, lost a net $239.9 million on Tuesday, November 17, with BlackRock’s IBIT accounting for $209.5 million. That came a day after IBIT’s first inflow in 11 sessions. Early figures pointed to further outflows on Wednesday.
 The miners aren’t giving up, though. The network’s hashrate , the total computing power securing Bitcoin, averaged about 1,015 exahashes per second over the past 30 days. That’s 9% below its November 2025 peak but 13% above its August low. Miners are still adding machines, a sign they expect higher prices later.

 BTC USD Price Analysis: The Mining Cost and $62,300 Sit Together
 On the daily chart, BTC USD trades at $63,879. That is below its 50-day exponential moving average (EMA), an average that gives recent prices more weight, at $75,252, and its 200-day EMA at $75,625.
 Support: $62,300, just below the $62,862 mining cost. Bitcoin bounced near it on Sunday and Wednesday, after it also held in February, June, July and August. Below it, $57,800, the July low.
 Resistance: $65,500, a level Bitcoin bounced from in early 2026 and was turned back from in June, July and August. Above that, $74,300.

 BTC USD has climbed back above the mining cost after all six dips this year. This time, miners are sellers and ETF money is leaving, so another recovery needs buyers to show up, not just sellers to stop.
